questions.text: Explain how plants are classified into herbs, shrubs, and trees, and give two examples of each.
questions.answer: Plants are classified by height and the type of stem. Herbs are short with soft, green stems (e.g., tulsi, mint). Shrubs are medium-sized with hard, branching stems near the ground (e.g., rose, lemon). Trees are tall with thick, woody stems and branches above the ground (e.g., mango, neem). This grouping helps in identifying and studying plants more easily.
questions.explanation: Tests understanding of plant classification by height and stem.

questions.text: Make a chart that classifies the following animals based on (a) habitat and (b) food: cow, eagle, frog, fish, lion, ant, sparrow.
questions.answer: By habitat — Land: cow, lion, ant. Air: eagle, sparrow. Water: fish. Both: frog. By food — Herbivore: cow. Carnivore: eagle, lion, sparrow (mainly insects/seeds), fish (varies). Omnivore: ant, frog. (Slight variations are acceptable; the student should explicitly use the two criteria and place each animal in valid groups.)
questions.explanation: Tests applying multiple grouping criteria to a real list.

questions.text: Write an essay (about 200 words) on 'Why we should protect biodiversity'. Include at least three concrete reasons, two examples of organisms, and two practical actions students can take.
questions.answer: Sample answer (open-ended). Biodiversity means the variety of plants, animals, and microorganisms found in nature. We need to protect it because: (1) It supports our food — bees pollinate crops; without them many fruits and vegetables would not grow. (2) It gives us medicines — many drugs come from plants like neem and tulsi. (3) It keeps the environment in balance — forests bring rain, soil microbes recycle waste. Animals like the tiger sit at the top of food chains and keep deer numbers in check; honeybees, though tiny, support farms across the country. Practical actions for students: plant local-species trees in school grounds, avoid throwing plastic into water bodies, and learn to identify and respect different kinds of insects instead of killing them out of fear. Conserving biodiversity is not just for far-away forests — it begins with how we treat the small piece of nature around us.
questions.explanation: Open-ended essay; full credit for clear reasons, examples, and actions.
